title: LARGE and SMALL: the nth highest

screens.prompt: Put the second-best time in the team into C2, keeping the list unsorted.

hints.syntax: LARGE takes the range and which one you want: =LARGE(B2:B6,2).
hints.func-large: MAX gives only the best time; the second best needs a function that counts in from the top.
hints.require-ref: Point at the column of times rather than listing them inside the formula.
hints.value: 2 means the second highest number, not the number in row 2: the answer is 58, not 61.
hints.error: Dividing by zero anywhere in the formula leaves #DIV/0!.

the best time, 61, rather than the one after it
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma means the arguments never separate

screens.prompt: Put the second-cheapest quote into C2 without re-sorting the table.

hints.syntax: SMALL is LARGE from the other end: =SMALL(B2:B6,2).
hints.func-small: MIN only knows the cheapest quote; the next one up needs a function that counts in from the bottom.
hints.require-ref: Read the range from B2:B6 so the quotes stay the only place the numbers live.
hints.value: 1 is the cheapest, 35; the second cheapest is 38.
hints.error: Dividing by zero replaces the quote with #DIV/0!.

the first quote is outside the range, so the count starts one place too high
the cheapest quote, 35, not the second cheapest

the missing comma leaves two arguments jammed into one

docs.explain: MAX and MIN answer only the first question anybody asks. The moment you want the runner-up, the third-worst month or the second-cheapest quote, you need a function that counts in from one end of the sorted order without sorting anything. LARGE does that from the top and SMALL from the bottom. The second argument is a position, not a row number, which is why 2 usually surprises people. The list stays exactly where it is: no helper column, no sort, no copy. Ranks that tie are counted separately, so two swimmers on 61 give LARGE 61 for both 1 and 2, and third place goes to the next distinct time. That is how Excel behaves, and it is worth knowing before a ranking report is published. A position beyond the size of the range returns #NUM! rather than a blank, so a chart title built on `=LARGE(...)` needs error handling if the list can shrink. The range should also be a range. LARGE over a hand-typed list freezes the answer and defeats the point.

errors.text: The position asked for is larger than the number of values in the range.
The position is zero or negative, so there is no such place in the order.
The range holds no numbers at all, so there is no order to count in from.

docs.atWork: A team sheet that names the second-best time, and a tender list that tracks the second-cheapest quote, both without re-sorting the underlying table.
docs.outcome: Pick the nth value in an unsorted list instead of sorting it to read one number.
docs.teaches: LARGE and SMALL with a position argument
docs.dataset: Swim times and five supplier quotes

seo.title: LARGE and SMALL in Excel: the nth value
seo.description: LARGE counts in from the top of an unsorted list and SMALL from the bottom, so the second argument is a position, not a row number. No sort needed.
